html:
The big picture

The built-in types (int, float, list, …) do not fit every problem: 1/2 + 2/3 as floats is not equal to 7/6. A class is a user-defined data type; its values are objects (instances). A class bundles two things: the instance variables (attributes) that hold each object's state, and the methods that operate on it, each receiving the object itself as the »zeroth« parameter self. The constructor __init__() sets up a new object. The data are kept private (double leading underscore __) and reached only through accessors (getters) and mutators (setters), so the class can guarantee its class invariant: the rules every object must satisfy after every method call (for Fraction: always reduced, positive denominator). Data that belong to the class as a whole live in class variables, read and written by class methods (marked with the decorator @classmethod). Dunder methods (__str__, __eq__, __add__, …) are hooks that let Python's own operators and conversions work on your objects; returning NotImplemented tells Python "I can't handle this operand". The lecture builds this up on one running example (Fraction, versions 0.2 → 1.2), then applies it to a stack (LIFO), a Sudoku class, a grayscale image class and a bouncing-ball simulation.

Classes as user-defined data types

Classes represent user-defined data types for special purposes that can be used similarly to the built-in data types. The »values« of these data types are called objects or instances (also: exemplars). A class can be considered as the description of its objects.

Example — fractions (rational numbers). Problem:

one_half    = 1/2
two_third   = 2/3
seven_sixth = 7/6
print("1/2+2/3 =", one_half + two_third)
print("7/6 =", seven_sixth)
print("are", "not" if one_half+two_third != seven_sixth else "", "equal")
1/2+2/3 = 1.1666666666666665
7/6 = 1.1666666666666667
are not equal

Side note on the slide: we need a data type that ensures that 1/2 + 2/3 = 7/6.

Connection

The two results differ in the last binary digit because float stores only an approximation of 1/2, 2/3 and 7/6 in binary (see Floating point numbers in 3 Variables, Data Types and Expressions). Each rounding is tiny, but 1/2 + 2/3 rounds twice and 7/6 once, so == sees two different bit patterns. A fraction type that stores two ints never rounds.

Class Fraction — look & feel

Basic concept for such a customised data type: manage numerator and denominator (each int) separately — do not divide! But »seen from outside«, a fraction should

  • look like »one« number and
  • be usable (almost) like a built-in data type, especially w.r.t. arithmetic:
one_half = Fraction(1, 2)
two_third = Fraction(2, 3)
sum = one_half.add(two_third)
print(sum.get_num(), "/", sum.get_den())   # get_num(): numerator of sum, get_den(): denominator of sum
7 / 6

(Slide: »this will become more comfortable soon…« — see version 1.1 below.)

Class Fraction — concept

Numerator and denominator are packed together in a data object of the class Fraction and managed as a unit. The class offers public operations that

  • initialise a fraction (assign numerator/denominator)
  • perform fraction arithmetic: +, −, *, /;
  • determine numerator or denominator;
  • convert fractions into strings (e.g., for output purposes)
  • convert fractions into float numbers
  • …

These operations access the internal data components.

Intuition

Think of the object as a sealed box with buttons. The numbers inside (the hidden data) can't be touched directly; you can only press the buttons on the outside (the methods). Because every change goes through a button, the box's designer can make sure the inside never gets into a nonsensical state. This idea of hiding the data behind operations is called encapsulation.

Class Fraction — attributes and methods

from __future__ import annotations     # needed for the type annotations with Fraction

class Fraction:
    def __init__ (self, n:int, d:int) -> None:
        self.__num = n
        self.__den = d

    def get_num (self) -> int:
        return self.__num

    def get_den (self) -> int:
        return self.__den

    def add (self, f:Fraction) -> Fraction:
        sum_num = self.__num * f.__den + self.__den * f.__num
        sum_den = self.__den * f.__den
        return Fraction(sum_num, sum_den)   # creates a new fraction as a result

Annotations on the slide:

  • Functions defined in classes are called methods; they have an additional »zeroth« parameter, typically called self, representing the object the method operates on. With one_half = Fraction(1, 2), the call passes one_half as self, 1 as n, 2 as d.
  • Initialisation method (constructor) __init__() — one of several specialised methods called dunder methods (»double underline«). Python constructors are always called __init__(). In Java & C++, constructors are named after the class (Fraction()), and objects of a class are created via the new operator: new Fraction(2, 3).
  • Define data by assignment: attributes __num and __den. Naming convention: a double leading underscore means »private« or »hidden from the outside«. In Java & C++, attributes must be declared: class Fraction { int num, den; }.
  • Define operations: methods get_num(), get_den() and add().
\frac{\text{num}}{\text{den}} + \frac{f.\text{num}}{f.\text{den}} = \frac{\text{num} \times f.\text{den} + \text{den} \times f.\text{num}}{\text{den} \times f.\text{den}}
Symbols
  • \text{num}, \text{den} — numerator and denominator of the object the method is called on (self.__num, self.__den); integers
  • f.\text{num}, f.\text{den} — numerator and denominator of the argument fraction f (f.__num, f.__den); integers
  • \times — integer multiplication; the result fraction has \text{den} \times f.\text{den} as common denominator
  • all quantities are dimensionless
Why may add() read f.__den, the private data of another object?

Privacy in Python is per class, not per object. Inside the body of class Fraction, every name of the form __x is rewritten by Python (name mangling) to _Fraction__x, so f.__den becomes f._Fraction__den — which exists, because f is also a Fraction. Outside the class no rewriting happens, so f.__den there looks for an attribute literally called __den and fails. Hence: code of the class may use the hidden data of all its objects; code outside may not.

Why is from __future__ import annotations needed?

The annotation f:Fraction in add is written inside the class body, while the class Fraction is still being defined, so the name Fraction does not exist yet. Without the import, Python evaluates annotations immediately and raises a NameError. The import makes Python store the annotations as text and evaluate them only when needed, when the class is complete.

Defining the structure of objects: attributes / instance variables

Classes manage »hidden data« that describe the state (content) of their objects (instances), e.g.,

  • numerator and denominator of a fraction
  • the 9×9 grid of a Sudoku puzzle
  • first name, last name, date of birth, … of a person

Such data (attributes) are stored in instance variables carried by each object (instance) of that class. (Slide: instance variables are the technical representations of attributes — in practice, both terms are used synonymously.)

Access to instance variables: object.instance_variable

Instance variables should generally not be directly accessed from outside the class, but kept private. Instead, methods should be used to access them. (Slide: we distinguish between private (standard) and public attributes (exception); more access specifications coming up later.)

In other languages, access to internal components (such as instance variables) from outside the class can be completely forbidden, e.g., by declaring them private:

class Fraction {
    private int num, den;
}

Defining the behaviour of objects: methods

Classes offer subroutines called methods that operate on their objects, e.g., get_num(), to_str(), add():

  • They may directly access »their« (the associated object's) instance variables
  • They can be called by other program parts (»clients«)

(Slide: we distinguish between public (standard) and private methods (exception); more access specifications coming up later.)

Call syntax: object.method(argument(s)) — the object is passed as the »zeroth« argument self, the arguments in parentheses as ordinary arguments #1, #2, …

class Fraction:
    # ... other stuff
    def get_num (self) -> int:
        return self.__num

    def get_den (self) -> int:
        return self.__den

f = Fraction(47, 11)
print(f.get_num(), "/", f.get_den())
47 / 11

Accessor (»getter«): method that returns information about the object (but does not change the object).

Objects — properties

Objects

  • represent the »values« of classes (like 7 for the type int);

  • are created from the classes via the class name:

    • Class() returns a reference to the new object of class Class (= address of the memory area in which the object was created);
    • object references can also point to nothing (None);
  • are (in Python) automatically »disposed of« when they are no longer needed (garbage collection);
  • consist of the instance variables corresponding to their attributes — these define the structure of the objects;
  • all have (the same) methods — these constitute their behavior and are defined in the object's class (Class);
  • communicate with each other by »sending messages« (message passing — conceptually; technically: by calling methods).
Connection

"Class() returns a reference" is the same memory model as for lists in 5 Sequence Types: g = f copies the reference, not the object, so f and g are two names for one Fraction. The prep course introduced the same ideas with a Bear class: 6 Classes and Objects.

Methods revisited — who is self?

Methods are subroutines that always operate on the object for which they are called (the object to the left of the dot):

f1 = Fraction(47, 11)
f2 = Fraction(7, 6)
d1 = f1.get_den()     # return self.__den in get_den() corresponds to f1.__den
d2 = f2.get_den()     # return self.__den in get_den() corresponds to f2.__den

This object is always passed as the leftmost (»zeroth«) argument, typically (but not necessarily — naming convention!) called self:

def get_den (self) -> int:
    return self.__den # self == f1 or f2, respectively (in the example)
Why does a method need self at all?

There is only one function get_den stored in the class, shared by all Fraction objects. To know whose denominator to return it must be told which object it is working on. f1.get_den() is shorthand for Fraction.get_den(f1): Python looks up get_den in the class of f1 and passes f1 as the first argument. Both calls return 11 for f1 = Fraction(47, 11).

Common mistake

Wrong: "self is passed automatically, so I don't need it in the definition" → writing def get_den():. Python still passes the object, so the call f1.get_den() fails with TypeError: … takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given. Also wrong: writing __den instead of self.__den inside a method — a bare name is a local variable, not the object's attribute. Right model: every instance method is defined with self first, and every access to the object's data inside it goes through self..

Constructors with optional parameters

If we want to generate fractions

  • from integers (k \to k/1)
  • completely without arguments (\to 0/1):
class Fraction:
    def __init__ (self, n:int=0, d:int=1):
        self.__num = n
        self.__den = d
    # ...

one_half = Fraction(1, 2)
print(one_half.get_num(), "/", one_half.get_den())
one = Fraction(1)
print(one.get_num(), "/", one.get_den())
zero = Fraction()
print(zero.get_num(), "/", zero.get_den())
1 / 2
1 / 1
0 / 1

Class Fraction version 0.2 — more methods

class Fraction:
    # ... (Constructor __init__() and accessors get_...() as before)

    def to_str (self) -> str:            # converts the fraction to a string
        return f"{self.__num}/{self.__den}"

    def to_float (self) -> float:        # converts the fraction to a float
        return self.__num / self.__den

    def add (self, f:Fraction) -> Fraction:   # adds the fraction to its argument f,
        sum_num = self.__num * f.__den + self.__den * f.__num   # returning a new fraction
        sum_den = self.__den * f.__den                           # as result (cf. before)
        return Fraction(sum_num, sum_den)

    def mult (self, f: Fraction) -> Fraction:
        return Fraction(self.__num * f.__num, self.__den * f.__den)

(Slide: in add, the auxiliary variables are unnecessary — compare mult.)

\frac{\text{num}}{\text{den}} \times \frac{f.\text{num}}{f.\text{den}} = \frac{\text{num} \times f.\text{num}}{\text{den} \times f.\text{den}}
Symbols

Symbols as above: \text{num}, \text{den} belong to self, f.\text{num}, f.\text{den} to the argument f; all integers, dimensionless.

    def sub (self, f:Fraction) -> Fraction:
        return Fraction(self.__num * f.__den - self.__den * f.__num,
                        self.__den * f.__den)

    def div (self, f: Fraction) -> Fraction:
        return Fraction(self.__num * f.__den, self.__den * f.__num)
\frac{\text{num}}{\text{den}} - \frac{f.\text{num}}{f.\text{den}} = \frac{\text{num} \times f.\text{den} - \text{den} \times f.\text{num}}{\text{den} \times f.\text{den}} \qquad \frac{\text{num}}{\text{den}} \div \frac{f.\text{num}}{f.\text{den}} = \frac{\text{num} \times f.\text{den}}{\text{den} \times f.\text{num}}
Symbols

Symbols as above. \div — division of fractions: multiply by the reciprocal \frac{f.\text{den}}{f.\text{num}} (only defined if f.\text{num} \neq 0).

# Test
two = Fraction(2)
one_third = Fraction(1, 3)
print(two.to_str())
print(one_third.add(one_third).to_str())
print(one_third.div(one_third).to_str())
2/1
6/9
3/3

Remarks on the slide: »/1« could be suppressed:

def to_str (self) -> str:
    return f"{self.__num}/{self.__den}" \
        if self.__den != 1 \
        else f"{self.__num}"

… and fractions should be reduced! (6/9 should be 2/3, 3/3 should be 1.)

Intuition

add, mult, sub and div never change self or f; each builds and returns a new Fraction. That makes a Fraction behave like an int: x + y doesn't modify x either. Objects whose methods never change them are easy to share between variables, because nobody can alter them behind your back (compare immutable tuple/str in 5 Sequence Types).

Class invariants — assertions for classes

Agreement on the design of class Fraction: »canonical form« of a Fraction object

  • __num/__den be always reduced
  • __den be always positive
  • 0 be always stored as 0/1
  • __den be never 0 (otherwise the fraction would be undefined)

(Slide: class invariants distinguish between »legal« and »illegal« objects, e.g. 0/3, 2/−3, 4/6, 7/0 … »illegal«; 0/1, −2/3, 2/3 … »legal«.)

A class invariant characterizes the »allowed state« of the objects of a class. It must (re)apply to every object of the class at the end of every method call.

Reducing a fraction: __num and __den are both divided by their greatest common divisor gcd(__num, __den).

Algorithm gcd(m, n) (as on the slide):

r ← m modulo n  (remainder of m/n)
While r > 0
    m ← n
    n ← r
    r ← m modulo n
gcd ← n

Riddle on the slide: what is the algorithm in Python?

Why does this loop find the greatest common divisor?

Write m = q \cdot n + r with r = m \bmod n. Any number that divides both m and n also divides r = m - q \cdot n; any number that divides both n and r also divides m = q \cdot n + r. So the pairs (m, n) and (n, r) have exactly the same common divisors, hence the same gcd. Each pass replaces the pair by a smaller one, and when the remainder reaches 0, n divides m, so the gcd is n itself. (This is Euclid's algorithm.) Example: (48, 18) \to (18, 12) \to (12, 6), remainder 0, gcd = 6.

Intuition

A class invariant is a promise the class makes about every one of its objects, like "a Fraction is always in lowest terms with a positive denominator". The constructor must establish it, and every method that changes the object must restore it before returning. In exchange, every method may rely on it, which simplifies code (see __eq__ in version 1.1). It is the class-level version of the assert checks from 4 Control Structures I.

Class Fraction version 1.0 — assuring the class invariants

from math import gcd    # Import greatest common divisor function

class Fraction:
    def __init__ (self, n:int=0, d:int=1):
        assert d != 0, "Denominator of a fraction must not be 0!"
        common_divisor = gcd(n, d) # Auxiliary function from math
        self.__num = n // common_divisor
        self.__den = d // common_divisor
        if self.__den < 0: # Denominator should not be negative
            self.__num = -self.__num
            self.__den = -self.__den
    # ... (everything else as before, to_str() improved)

# Test (same as before)
two = Fraction(2)
one_third = Fraction(1, 3)
print(two.to_str())
print(one_third.add(one_third).to_str())
print(one_third.div(one_third).to_str())
2
2/3
1

(Slide: at the end of __init__, the object self is in canonical form.)

Worked example — tracing the constructor for Fraction(2, -4) and Fraction(0, 5)
  1. Guard the invariant "denominator ≠ 0": d = -4, so the assert passes.
  2. Reduce: gcd(2, -4) is 2 (math.gcd always returns a non-negative number), so __num = 2 // 2 = 1, __den = -4 // 2 = -2.
  3. Make the denominator positive: -2 < 0, so both signs flip → __num = -1, __den = 2. Result -1/2: legal.
  4. Zero: Fraction(0, 5): gcd(0, 5) = 5 → 0 // 5 = 0, 5 // 5 = 1 → stored as 0/1, exactly as the invariant demands, with no special case needed. (Checked by running the class: Fraction(2, -4) prints -1/2, Fraction(0, 5) prints 0.)

By manipulating an object's attributes directly (by assignment to its instance variables), the class invariants (here: the canonical form of a fraction) can easily be violated:

f = Fraction(1, 6)
print(f.to_str())
f.__num = 2
print(f.to_str())
1/6
2/6

Slide annotations: »This statement only shows the intent to change the fraction. It does not work as expected because of the double underline signalling »privacy«.« — »f is not in canonical form anymore (should be 1/3).«

Unclear (slide 185)

The printed output 2/6 shows the intended effect, not what Python actually prints. Run as written, the second line prints 1/6 again: outside the class, f.__num = 2 is not name-mangled, so it creates a new, unrelated attribute called __num on f (checked: vars(f) afterwards is {'_Fraction__num': 1, '_Fraction__den': 6, '__num': 2}). The slide's own note ("does not work as expected because of the double underline") points at this. The lesson is unchanged: direct assignment could break the invariant if it reached the real attribute (e.g. via f._Fraction__num = 2, which really does give 2/6).

Therefore, if we want to modify an object from outside its class, we should introduce appropriate methods (mutators, »setters«) that know about and obey the class invariants:

class Fraction:
    def set_num (self, new_n:int) -> None: # Mutator method
        self.__num = new_n    # Change object
        self.__canonicalize() # Bring self in canonical form again
    # ...

The full version 1.0 with a private auxiliary method:

class Fraction:
    def __canonicalize (self) -> None:
        assert self.__den != 0, \
            "Denominator = 0!"
        common_divisor = gcd(self.__num, self.__den)
        self.__num //= common_divisor
        self.__den //= common_divisor
        if self.__den < 0:
            self.__num = -self.__num
            self.__den = -self.__den

    def __init__ (self, n:int=0, d:int=1) -> None:
        self.__num = n
        self.__den = d
        self.__canonicalize()

    def set_num (self, new_n:int) -> None: # Mutator method
        self.__num = new_n    # Change object
        self.__canonicalize() # Bring self in canonical form
    # ...
  • __canonicalize() is a private (hence the double underscore!) auxiliary method that brings the object (self) in canonical form (a state where all class invariants hold). It can also be used by the constructor. (Slide: »this name is not standard … just a Hitz idea«.)
  • Components named with (at least one) leading _ should not be used outside of the class — not even methods!
  • Instance variables should generally not be accessed from outside the class; methods should be used instead. This is especially true when changing the object: use mutator methods (setters) instead!
Common mistake

Wrong: "A double underscore makes the attribute truly private, like private in Java." Why it fails: Python only renames __x to _ClassName__x inside the class; anyone can still reach f._Fraction__num, and assigning f.__num from outside silently creates a second attribute (slide 185). Right model: __ is a strong convention plus a rename that prevents accidents. The class's correctness still depends on clients using only its public methods.

Example: stack memory — a classical example

Stack: a special type of data structure.

Properties:

  • Stores any number of elements of the same type
  • Accessible is always only the last inserted (top) (»Last In – First Out«, LIFO)

Classical operations:

  • push(e): places element e on top of the stack
  • top(): returns the top stack element
  • pop(): returns and removes the top stack element
  • size(): returns the number of stack elements
  • is_empty(): checks whether the stack is empty

Using a stack

Assumption: class Stack implements a stack.

s = Stack() # Will be used as stack of float elements
running = True
while running:
    print("size:", s.size(),
          "top:", "<empty>" if s.is_empty() else s.top())
    input_str = input("Command or number: ")
    if input_str == "exit":
        running = False
    elif input_str == "pop":
        print(s.pop())
    else: # input_str hopefully holds a number...
        s.push(float(input_str)) # ... to be pushed
size: 0 top: <empty>
Command or number: 47
size: 1 top: 47.0
Command or number: 11
size: 2 top: 11.0
Command or number: pop
11.0
size: 1 top: 47.0
Command or number: pop
47.0
size: 0 top: <empty>
Command or number: exit
Intuition

A stack is a pile of plates: you put a plate on top and take one from the top; the plate at the bottom is the first one in and the last one out. Notice the program above uses the stack without knowing how it is built: it only calls push, pop, top, size, is_empty. That separation between what a class offers and how it does it is the payoff of encapsulation. In computing, the same structure keeps track of function calls (the call stack) and of "undo" histories.

Stack implementation based on a list

class Stack:
    def __init__ (self) -> None:
        self.__data = [] # List of stacked elements

    def push (self, item) -> None:
        self.__data.append(item)

    def pop (self):
        assert not self.is_empty()
        return self.__data.pop()

    def top (self):
        assert not self.is_empty()
        return self.__data[-1] # Last element of list

    def is_empty (self) -> bool:
        return self.size() == 0

    def size (self) -> bool:
        return len(self.__data)

Riddle on the slide: re-implement class Stack with the top element at the beginning of the list.

Unclear (slide 189)

size() is annotated -> bool, but it returns len(self.__data), an int. The annotation should be -> int (Python ignores annotations at run time, so the program still works; a type checker such as mypy would complain).

Why does the list version keep the top at the end of the list?

append and pop() without an index work at the end of a list and take the same short time however long the list is. Adding or removing at the front (insert(0, …), pop(0)) forces Python to shift every other element one place, so it gets slower as the stack grows. Both versions behave identically from the outside; only the cost differs.

Common mistake

Wrong: creating the list once in the class body, class Stack: __data = [], instead of in __init__. Why it fails: a variable in the class body is a class variable (next section), so all stacks share one list: after a.push(1), an unrelated stack b also has size 1 (checked by script). Right model: per-object state is created in __init__ with self.… = …, so every object gets its own list.

Class variables

Assume we want to know the number of Fraction objects generated by our program. We could introduce a counter that is incremented whenever a new Fraction object is created, i.e., whenever the constructor of class Fraction is executed. However, such a counter would have to be a variable shared by all Fraction objects — thus, it should be an attribute of the whole class rather than of an individual object.

Use class variables when:

  • A value should be shared among all instances (e.g., global counters/settings).
  • The data logically belongs to the class itself, not individual objects (e.g., constants).

We call such attributes class attributes. They are implemented by class variables (in contrast to the instance variables discussed so far). They belong to the class, not to its instances.

In Python, class variables (implementations of class attributes) are defined inside the class but outside of any instance methods.

class Fraction:
    counter = 0 # Define and initialize a class variable (class attribute)
    def __init__ (self, n:int=0, d:int=1):
        self.__num = n
        self.__den = d
        self.__canonicalize()
        Fraction.counter += 1
    # ...

print(Fraction.counter) # Access without creating an object
f = Fraction(47, 11)
print(f.counter) # Access via object – works, but is not recommended
                 # (looks like an instance variable!)
0
1

In Java and C++, class variables are defined as static:

class Fraction {
    private int num, den;
    static int counter = 0;
    // ...
}
Common mistake

Wrong: incrementing with self.counter += 1 in __init__. Why it fails: self.counter += 1 means self.counter = self.counter + 1. Reading self.counter finds the class variable (0), but the assignment creates a new instance variable counter on that one object. The class's counter stays 0 forever (checked: after one call, class value 0, instance value 1). Right model: write class variables through the class name, Fraction.counter += 1, as on the slide. This is also why the slide discourages reading them via an object.

Class methods

If we want to encapsulate also class variables, we need getter and setter methods for these attributes — these class methods must also work without an instance:

class Fraction:
    counter = 0

    @classmethod # Decorator modifying get_counter()
    def get_counter (cls):      # Argument:
        return cls.counter      # cls = class, not self!
    #   return Fraction.counter   (alternative)
    # ...

print(Fraction.get_counter()) # Access without object
f = Fraction(47, 11)
print(f.get_counter()) # Access via object – works,
                       # but is not recommended
                       # (looks like calling an
                       # instance method!)
0
1

A decorator is a special function that modifies another function or method without changing its actual code. Decorators are prefixed with @ and are placed directly above the function/method they modify.

In Java and C++, class methods are defined as static:

class Fraction {
    private int num, den;
    static int counter = 0;
    static int getCounter () {
        return counter;
    }
    // ...
}
Why does a class method receive cls instead of self?

A class method can be called as Fraction.get_counter() with no object at all, so there is no self to pass. @classmethod changes the call so that Python passes the class as the first argument instead. Through cls the method can reach class variables (cls.counter) but no instance variables, since there's no particular object to read them from. Using cls instead of the hard-coded Fraction is what the slide's "alternative" line contrasts.

Methods revisited — summary

Depending on the tasks of a class' methods, we distinguish:

  • Constructors: initialize a newly created (instantiated) object (__init__())
  • Accessors (»Getter methods«): read and return parts of the object
  • Mutators (»Setter methods«): modify parts of the object
  • Destructors: are called when an object ceases to exist — rarely used in Python (__del__(), cf. possibly later)

From a structural perspective, we distinguish:

  • Instance methods (or simply: methods): work with the status of an object (with instance variables), may also access class variables
  • Class methods: work only at class level (with class variables) — have no access to objects and their instance variables
Worked example — designing a small class with an invariant

Task: a 24-hour Clock showing hh:mm. Steps, each labelled by purpose:

  1. Choose the hidden state: one instance variable __minutes (minutes since midnight) — one number is easier to keep consistent than two.
  2. State the invariant: 0 <= __minutes < 1440.
  3. Constructor establishes it: reduce modulo 1440.
  4. Mutator restores it: same reduction after every change.
  5. Conversion via a dunder method so print works (next section).
class Clock:
    def __init__ (self, h:int=0, m:int=0) -> None:   # constructor
        self.__minutes = (h*60 + m) % (24*60)
    def add_minutes (self, m:int) -> None:            # mutator
        self.__minutes = (self.__minutes + m) % (24*60)
    def __str__ (self) -> str:                         # conversion
        return f"{self.__minutes // 60:02}:{self.__minutes % 60:02}"
c = Clock(23, 50); c.add_minutes(25); print(c)        # 00:15

Checked by running: Clock(23, 50) → 23:50, after add_minutes(25) → 00:15, Clock(25, 70) → 02:10, Clock(0, -10) → 23:50 (Python's % is never negative for a positive divisor).

Class Fraction version 1.1 — implicit conversion

So far, conversion to str or float needs to be called explicitly (f.to_str(), f.to_float()). This can also be »automated« by defining two special »dunder functions«:

class Fraction:
    # ... (as before)
    def __str__ (self) -> str:
        return self.to_str()

    def __float__ (self) -> float:
        # Enables conversion using the built-in float() function
        return self.to_float()

For implicit type conversion to the data type str, the method __str__() is automatically called for objects of any class!

two = Fraction(2)
one_third = Fraction(1, 3)
print(two)               # Fraction object two is converted to str by an implicit call to two.__str__()
print(float(one_third))  # conversion function float() calls one_third.__float__()
2
0.3333333333333333
Intuition

Dunder methods are hooks: places where Python's own machinery calls your code. print(x) and f"{x}" need a string, so they ask the object for one via x.__str__(); float(x) asks via x.__float__(). Without __str__, print(two) would print something like <__main__.Fraction object at 0x10…>, the default text every object inherits.

Class Fraction version 1.1 — implicit comparison

To compare two fractions, we either convert them to float first (if float(f1) > float(f2):) — again facing the problem of loss of precision — or implement the dunder functions that Python calls implicitly when objects appear between operators like == or <:

OperatorMethod name
== (Equality)__eq__(self, other)
!= (Inequality)__ne__(self, other)
< (Less than)__lt__(self, other)
<= (Less than or equal)__le__(self, other)
> (Greater than)__gt__(self, other)
>= (Greater than or equal)__ge__(self, other)
\frac{\text{num}}{\text{den}} = \frac{f.\text{num}}{f.\text{den}} \iff \text{num} \times f.\text{den} = \text{den} \times f.\text{num}
Symbols
  • \text{num}, \text{den} — numerator and denominator of self; f.\text{num}, f.\text{den} — of the other fraction (other in the code); integers, dimensionless
  • \iff — "if and only if": the two statements are equivalent (valid because both denominators are non-zero)
class Fraction:
    # ... (as before)
    def __eq__(self, other:Fraction): # Equality: self == other
        return self.__num * other.__den == self.__den * other.__num
        # Since we know that our objects fulfill all class invariants,
        # we could also use this statement:
        # return self.__num == other.__num and self.__den == other.__den

    def __lt__(self, other:Fraction): # Less than: self < other
        return self.__num * other.__den < self.__den * other.__num

# Test
two = Fraction(2)
one_third = Fraction(1, 3)
print(one_third < two)    # calls one_third.__lt__(two)
print(one_third == two)   # calls one_third.__eq__(two)
True
False

Riddle on the slide: implement the complete table from the previous slide.

Why may __eq__ simply compare numerators and denominators, thanks to the invariant?

Every rational number has exactly one reduced form with a positive denominator. Because the class invariant guarantees that every Fraction is stored in that form, two Fractions are equal as numbers exactly when their stored numerators and denominators are equal. Without the invariant, 2/4 and 1/2 would be stored differently and the shortcut would wrongly call them unequal; the cross-multiplication test works in both cases.

Why is __lt__ allowed to cross-multiply?

\frac{a}{b} < \frac{c}{d} becomes a \cdot d < c \cdot b by multiplying both sides by b \cdot d. Multiplying an inequality keeps its direction only if the factor is positive. The invariant "denominator always positive" guarantees b \cdot d > 0. With a negative denominator allowed, the test would give wrong answers, so here the invariant is not just tidiness: the method's correctness depends on it.

Class Fraction version 1.1 — implicit arithmetic

Python also supports dunder methods to map operators *, +, etc. to methods like mult(), add(), etc.:

OperatorMethod name
+__add__(self, other)
–__sub__(self, other)
*__mul__(self, other)
/__truediv__(self, other)
class Fraction:
    # ... (as before)
    def __add__(self, other:Fraction):
        return self.add(other)
    # etc.

# Test
one_third = Fraction(1, 3)
print(one_third + one_third)   # calls one_third.__add__(one_third)
2/3

Slide notes: we could also deal with other data types, e.g., int as in one_third + 7 (omitted for sake of clarity). Riddle: implement the complete table.

Worked example — what Python does for print(one_third + one_third)
  1. Operator → hook: + with a Fraction on the left becomes one_third.__add__(one_third).
  2. Hook → arithmetic: __add__ calls self.add(other): numerator 1 \cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 1 = 6, denominator 3 \cdot 3 = 9, so Fraction(6, 9) is constructed.
  3. Invariant: the constructor reduces by gcd(6, 9) = 3 → stored as 2/3.
  4. Conversion hook: print needs a string → __str__() → to_str() → "2/3". Four of the chapter's ideas (operator dunder, method call, invariant in the constructor, conversion dunder) meet in one line.

Class Fraction version 1.2 — implicit comparison & arithmetic with mixed operands

What happens if we try to compare a Fraction object with a non-Fraction operand?

one_third = Fraction(1, 3)
print(one_third == 7)

It fails:

File "Fraction.py", line 139, in <module>
  print(one_third == 7)
        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
File "Fraction.py", line 65, in __eq__
  return self.__num * other.__den == self.__den *
other.__num
                      ^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute '__den'

The same is true for other operands like < or + etc. We can mitigate the problem by …

… checking the data type of the second argument:

  • return False if the second argument is not of type Fraction, or
  • try to convert the argument and come up with a meaningful result.
class Fraction:
    # ...
    def __eq__ (self, other): # Equality: self == other
        if isinstance(other, Fraction):
            return self.__num * other.__den == self.__den * other.__num
        return NotImplemented # Can't compare with other types

one_third = Fraction(1, 3)
print(one_third == 7)
f = Fraction(7)
print(f == 7)
False
False
  • isinstance(object, type) yields True if object is an instance of type.
  • At the end of the evaluation of the comparison, Python maps NotImplemented to False!
  • We could argue that f == 7 should yield True.

Hence the extended version:

class Fraction:
    # ...
    def __eq__ (self, other): # Equality: self == other
        if isinstance(other, Fraction):
            return self.__num * other.__den == self.__den * other.__num
        if isinstance(other, int):
            return self.__num == other and self.__den == 1
        if isinstance(other, float):
            return self.to_float() == other
        return NotImplemented # other is incompatible

one_third = Fraction(1, 3)
f = Fraction(7)
print(one_third == 7)
print(f == 7)
print(f == 7.0)
print(7 == f)
print(f == "7")
False
True
True
True
False

How 7 == f is evaluated (slide): Python first attempts int.__eq__(7, f). Since int.__eq__() does not know how to compare an int to a Fraction, it returns NotImplemented. Since int.__eq__() returned NotImplemented, Python automatically retries the comparison in reverse: f.__eq__(7). This now calls the Fraction.__eq__() method, which correctly handles integers, so it returns True.

Riddle on the slide: complete this logic for the 3 Fraction operators introduced earlier.

Intuition

NotImplemented is not an error and not False; it is a polite "not my job" that a dunder method hands back to Python. Python then gives the other operand a chance. Only if both sides decline does Python fall back to a default. Raising an exception or returning False instead would block that second chance, which is why 7 == f works only because Fraction.__eq__ is reached through the retry.

Common mistake

Wrong: "NotImplemented always ends up as False." Why it fails: that fallback exists only for == and != (they then compare identity). For <, <=, >, >= and arithmetic, if both sides return NotImplemented Python raises a TypeError, e.g. Fraction(1, 3) < 7 → TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'Fraction' and 'int' (checked). Right model: NotImplemented passes the question to the other operand; if nobody answers, ==/!= fall back to "same object?", everything else is an error.

Common mistake

Wrong: return NotImplementedError or raise NotImplemented. Why it fails: NotImplementedError is an exception class meant for "this method isn't written yet"; returning it gives a truthy object, so f == "7" would look True. Right model: comparison and arithmetic dunders return the special value NotImplemented (no Error).

Grayscale images — basic image processing

Concept: a grayscale image is an int matrix of pixels with the values 0 (black) to 255 (white, 0xFF). Row 0 / column 0 is the top left corner. (The slide shows an example image with 256 rows with values from 0 to 255, all columns equal: a vertical gradient from black at the top to white at the bottom.)

Run pip install pillow first.

We use an auxiliary class Image from the Pillow library for creating images, reading and writing image files, changing pixel values, and displaying the images:

from PIL import Image
image = Image.new("L", (256, 256)) # "L": grayscale, (width, height)
for x in range(image.width):
    for y in range(image.height):
        image.putpixel((x, y), y)   # set pixel at position (x, y) to the value of the 2nd argument (0-255, here y)
image.show()

Reading a pixel value at position (x, y) is done with image.getpixel((x, y)).

Class GrayScaleImage manages a grayscale image — initially load/create, display, save:

class GrayScaleImage:
    BLACK, WHITE = 0, 0xFF       # class variables (conceptually constant → capitals!)

    def __init__ (self, info:str|tuple[int, int]) -> None:
        if isinstance(info, str): # info is a file name
            self.__image = Image.open(info).convert("L")   # load picture file and return Image object; "L" means grayscale (0-255)
        elif isinstance(info, tuple): # info is (width, height)
            self.__image = Image.new("L", info)            # initially all black pixels
        else: assert False
    def show (self) -> None: self.__image.show()
    def save (self, filename:str) -> None: self.__image.save(filename)

Further behavior?

  • Accessors
  • Mutators: image processing (rotation, contrast, exposure, negative, …)
Connection

GrayScaleImage wraps Pillow's Image: its instance variable __image holds a reference to an object of another class, and its methods delegate to it (show → self.__image.show()). Objects built from other objects is how larger programs are put together. The constructor accepts two kinds of argument and tells them apart with isinstance, the same tool as in Fraction.__eq__. The starter file GrayScaleImage.py (in GrayScale.zip) already contains binarize and rotate_right as examples, plus empty stubs for the exercise ideas below. Images as integer matrices are also how a robot's camera frames reach your code.

Intuition

Ideas for exercises (riddles for merit points)

Blur (riddle: 2 merit points)

  • Replace each pixel with the average of the pixel values of all 3–8 neighbors and the original pixel. (Figure: the tree photo before and after blurring.)
  • (Riddle: 1 additional merit point) Use a weighted average for the mean: environment·(1−w) + pixel·w (w = 0 → pixel no longer plays a role at all, w = 1 → no effect).
\text{newpixel} = w \cdot \text{pixel} + (1 - w) \cdot \frac{\sum_{p \in \text{neighbors}} p}{\lvert \text{neighbors} \rvert}
Symbols
  • \text{newpixel} — the pixel's gray value after blurring (0–255)
  • \text{pixel} — the pixel's original gray value (0–255)
  • w — weight of the original pixel, 0 \le w \le 1; w = 1: no change, w = 0: pure neighbourhood average
  • \text{neighbors} — the set of pixels adjacent to this one (horizontally, vertically, diagonally): 8 inside the image, 5 on an edge, 3 in a corner
  • \sum_{p \in \text{neighbors}} p — sum of the gray values p of all neighbours
  • \lvert \text{neighbors} \rvert — number of neighbours (3, 5 or 8)

Grayscale spread (riddle: 2 merit points)

  • Define a gray value black (≥ BLACK) to be mapped to black and a gray value white (≤ WHITE) to be mapped to white

  • Transform the gray value of all pixels accordingly:

    • values ≤ black → BLACK
    • values ≥ white → WHITE
    • linearly transform other values x between black and white: → (x – black) / (white – black) * 255
x' = \frac{x - \text{black}}{\text{white} - \text{black}} \cdot 255 \qquad (\text{black} < x < \text{white})
Symbols
  • x — a pixel's original gray value (0–255)
  • x' — its new gray value after the spread (0–255; round or truncate to an int before storing)
  • \text{black} — the chosen gray value that becomes pure black (BLACK = 0); \text{white} — the chosen gray value that becomes pure white (WHITE = 255); need \text{black} < \text{white}
  • 255 — WHITE, the largest gray value
Worked example — reading the spread formula, spread(50, 205)
  1. Classify each value: 30 ≤ 50 → BLACK (0); 220 ≥ 205 → WHITE (255); 128 lies in between → formula.
  2. Shift so black becomes 0: 128 - 50 = 78.
  3. Scale the range 155 to 255: \frac{78}{205 - 50} \cdot 255 = \frac{78}{155} \cdot 255 \approx 128.3, stored as 128.
  4. Sanity check the ends: x = 50 gives 0 and x = 205 gives 255, so the formula meets the two clipping rules without a jump.

Histogram of the grayscale distribution (riddle: 3 merit points)

  • Count the number of occurrences of gray values from BLACK to WHITE (→ 256 counts).
  • Create a new grayscale image with (e.g.) 256 columns j, containing black bars with height corresponding to the number of occurrences of the gray value j.

Solarization (riddle: 2 merit points)

  • Compute the maximum difference d of gray values of a pixel and its 3–8 neighboring pixels
  • If d > threshold (user-defined): pixel → BLACK, otherwise: pixel → WHITE
Intuition

Solarization as defined here is an edge detector: a pixel turns black only where gray values change sharply around it (a branch against the sky), and white where the area is smooth. The threshold decides how sharp a change must be to count, which is why SOL(20) marks more texture than SOL(60).

Simulation — bouncing balls as individual objects: class UBO

class UBO: # Unidentified Bouncing Object
    def __init__ (self, color:str="", pos:tuple[float,float], r:float): -> None:
        self.__r = r              # Ball size (radius)
        self.__pos = pos          # Ball position
        self.__v = (0.025 - random()/20, 0.025 - random()/20) # Ball velocity
        self.__color = color if color else Graph.rand_color()

    def step (self) -> None:      # Single simulation step
        x, y = self.__pos         # Fetch instance variables...
        vx, vy = self.__v         # ...for notational convenience
        if math.fabs(x + vx) + self.__r > 1.0: # Hits right or left wall
            vx = -vx              # Invert horizontal movement component
        if math.fabs(y + vy) + self.__r > 1.0: # Hits upper or lower wall
            vy = -vy              # Invert vertical movement component
        x += vx                   # Move one step
        y += vy
        self.__pos = (x, y)       # Restore modified instance variables
        self.__v = (vx, vy)
Unclear (slide 210)

The constructor header as printed is not valid Python: pos and r have no default values although they follow color:str="" (a parameter without a default may not follow one with a default), and ): -> None: has a stray colon before ->. The file UBO.py in UBO.zip has the working header def __init__ (self, color:str="", pos:tuple[float,float]=(0,0), r:float=0.04):, which also matches the main program calling UBO(color=…, r=…) without pos.

    def draw (self) -> None:       # Draw object
        Graph.circle(*self.__pos, self.__r, fill_color=self.__color)

    __universe:list = []           # Class variable: All known UBOs

    @classmethod
    def universe (cls) -> list[UBO]:
        return cls.__universe

    @classmethod
    def add (cls, ubo:UBO) -> None: # Put a UBO into the universe
        cls.__universe.append(ubo)
Intuition

Each ball is its own object with its own position, velocity, size and colour, and knows how to move (step) and draw itself (draw). The main loop never touches a ball's data; it just tells every ball "step, then draw". The set of all balls is one class variable __universe, shared by all UBOs, reached through the class methods universe() and add(). Here sharing one list is exactly what is wanted (contrast the stack mistake above). In step, each velocity component flips sign when the next move would take the ball's edge past the wall at \pm 1: that is the bounce.

Main program (simulation)

Graph.create("Unidentified Bouncing Objects", 700, 700)
Graph.set_scale(-1, 1, -1, 1)

running:bool = True
singlestep = 0    # Number of single-step simulations - 0 -> off
pause = 0.02      # Waiting 0.02 seconds between simulation steps (speed 4)
while running:    # Update positions and draw objects
    Graph.clear() # Clear old picture
    for ubo in UBO.universe():
        ubo.step()
        ubo.draw()

    if singlestep:
        Graph.show(f"ENTER to continue with {singlestep} single-steps")
        singlestep -= 1
    else:        # Continuous mode
        Graph.show(pause)

Main program (user input)

    if input_available():        # Non-blocking input – see next slide
        user_input = get_input().split()    # List of strings
        n = len(user_input)

            match user_input[0]:

Tools for non-blocking input

import sys
import platform
if platform.system() == "Windows":
    import msvcrt

    def input_available() -> bool:
        return msvcrt.kbhit()

    def get_input() -> str:
        line = ""
        while True:
            char = msvcrt.getwch()
            if char == '\r': # ENTER
                print()
                break
            elif char == '\b': # ←
                line = line[:-1]
                sys.stdout.write("\b \b")
                sys.stdout.flush()
            else: # Ordinary character
                line += char
                sys.stdout.write(char)
                sys.stdout.flush()
        return line.strip()
else: # UNIX / MacOSX
    import select

    def input_available() -> bool:
        return select.select([sys.stdin],
                             [], [], 0)[0] != []

    def get_input() -> str:
        return sys.stdin.readline().strip()
Why does the simulation need non-blocking input?

The ordinary input() blocks: the program stops and waits until the user presses Enter, so the balls would freeze between commands. input_available() only checks whether something has been typed (on Windows msvcrt.kbhit(), on macOS/Linux select with a timeout of 0) and returns at once, so the loop keeps animating and reads a command only when one is waiting. The two branches exist because the operating systems offer different tools for this check.
